title: Eleven Fifty-Nine

pages.text:
At 4:10, the sprinkler fired.

Mr. Grady’s lawn is next door, and his sprinkler is a chaotic, spinning thing that treats the mailman as a personal enemy. I watched from the roof as the mailman, a man in a blue uniform who looked like he had already lost three fights today, stepped into the spray.

The water hit him with the sudden, freezing shock of dropping an ice cube directly into a glass of warm soda. He didn’t scream; he just stood there, soaking, while the sprinkler continued its merry dance. Then he yelled. It was a good yell, the kind that comes from a place where dignity went to die.

I almost laughed. The feeling bubbled up in my throat, hot and sharp, but I swallowed it down like a pill I didn't want to take. It was the only thing all day that had almost made me smile, and I hated it for that.

Then I heard Mom’s voice below.

"Max! Dinner! It’s the last supper in this house, so please come down and be a human being for five minutes!"

I looked at the mailman, now walking away with his head hanging low. I looked at the pretzels in my hand. I hopped down the side of the garage.

The last supper. Okay. I could do that. I could do five minutes of being a human being. Probably.
pages.image: Max on a dusty garage roof peering down at Mr. Grady's sprinkler soaking the mailman in blue uniform; afternoon light, suburban street, Max looking conflicted.

pages.text:
The living room felt hollow, like a cereal box with the contents scooped out. We sat in a circle on the floor, surrounded by a pyramid of pizza boxes and paper plates. Dad stood up, holding a slice of pepperoni high in the air.

"To the house," he said. "To Ohio. To new cactus adventures."

We clinked our lemonade bottles together. The sound was flat and plastic, more like tapping a phone screen than a celebration.

Mom wasn’t making a scene, but she was staring at her clipboard, which she had dragged to the floor. She kept checking a box, then checking it again, her pencil moving in tight little circles that didn’t match up with anything on the list.

Gus had a slice of pizza sticking out of the mouth hole in his T. rex hood. It looked like a dinosaur trying to talk through a mouthful of cheese. He seemed genuinely happy, which made me feel a little more grumpy than before.

Tessa sat right next to me. She wasn’t looking at anyone. She was watching her hands, and I could hear the dull thud of her drumsticks tapping against her thigh. *Tap. Tap. Tap.*

She didn’t say hi. She didn’t say bye. She just sat there, purple streak of hair and all, keeping her distance like she was waiting for the rest of the world to leave.
pages.image: Family sitting in a circle on an empty living room floor with pizza boxes; Dad raising a pizza slice, Mom looking at a clipboard, Gus with pizza in his T. rex hood, Tessa staring at her hands.

pages.text:
"Okay," Mom said. Her voice had a wobble in it, like a dog trying to bark through a full mouth. "One thing you’ll miss. Go around."

Dad went first. "The kitchen," he announced, his face bright. "Specifically, the fridge light. It’s the only good thing in this house."

Tessa went next. She didn’t look up. "My drum room," she whispered, tapping her sticks against her knee in a quiet, steady rhythm.

Gus went third. "Everything," he said, his voice muffled by a slice of pepperoni. "Even the stairs. The ones that go up and down."

Then it was my turn. The circle waited. Dad looked at me. Mom looked at me. Gus looked at me with his pizza-tongue.

I wanted to say something nice. I wanted to mention the backyard, or the creek, or Jonah’s house. But the words got stuck in my throat like a gummy bear that had turned to plastic. Instead, what came out of my mouth was this: "Nothing. Because it’s all going to be worse there."

Silence fell over the living room, heavy and thick as a wet blanket. Waffles chewed on the corner of the pizza box. *Crunch. Crunch.*

Mom didn’t yell. She just looked at me with eyes that were very tired and very sad.

"Go to bed, Max," she said softly. "Early."

"Glady," I said. And I meant it.
pages.image: Max sitting stiffly on the floor between his parents and siblings, looking defensive; Waffles the corgi chewing the corner of a pizza box nearby; dim evening light.

pages.text:
My room was an air mattress in a box.

I lay on my back staring at a ceiling that was just white, the kind of blank, featureless white that looks like a sheet of printer paper taped to the sky. There were no posters, no rocket lamp, no pale rectangles where my six years of life had been. Just the flat, empty surface.

The house breathed around me. I could hear Dad snoring in the next room, a low rumble that sounded like a diesel truck stuck in second gear, while Mom’s pencil scratched on paper in the hall with the soft, anxious rhythm of someone trying to keep the world from falling apart.

Then there was Tessa. Her drumsticks tapped against the wall, *tap, tap, tap*, a slow, steady beat that felt less like music and more like a countdown to something I didn't want to hear.

I wasn't afraid of the dark, because I wasn't. I was afraid of the truck. I was afraid of waking up and seeing it there, the engine idling, the boxes gone, and me being a person who lived in Tucson, Arizona, instead of Dunmore, Ohio. I was afraid of never getting to be the kid who knew which streetlight flickered before the rain.

The tapping stopped.

Dad’s snoring got louder.

I closed my eyes.
pages.image: Max lying on an air mattress in a bare room, staring at the white ceiling; shadows of moving boxes in the corner; quiet, lonely atmosphere.

pages.text:
It was 11:58.

I shouldn't have been awake, but I was, which is usually the first sign that the night has gone sideways. The house was silent except for the house itself, settling and ticking. Moonlight poured through the glass door in the front hall, pooling on the floor like spilled milk.

The clock hung on its hook. It ticked.

I stood under it, looking up at Gerald. He was in his little wooden house, behind the door. I could see one eye, black and round, watching me with the judgmental glare of a teacher who knows you haven't done your homework.

"I wish today would never end," I whispered.

The door popped open with a *fwoop*.

Gerald came out. His beak was crooked. His eyebrows were angry. He looked at me, then he made a sound.

*Cuck-oo.*

Just one. Not three. Not four. Just one crooked cuckoo, lonely and off-key like a kid singing "Happy Birthday" to no one.

It was 11:59.

I laughed. It was a short, dry laugh, the kind that comes out when you trip over your own feet in the cafeteria. I felt stupid. I felt like a kid who had made a wish at a wishing well and gotten a single, flat penny.

I went back to bed.

I fell asleep smiling.

Which should have been my first clue.
pages.image: Max standing in a dark hallway looking up at a cuckoo clock on a hook; moonlight streaming through a glass door; Gerald the cuckoo bird peering out with a crooked beak.
